item.title: Pinglu Canal opens, creating a new gateway to the sea for southwest China
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
On September 16, the Pinglu Canal officially opens to navigation. This 134.2-kilometer canal connects the main channel of the Xijiang River with the Beibu Gulf, giving southwest China a more direct route to the sea.

item.title: Chinese FM holds phone talks with Rubio on high-level interactions
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke by phone on Thursday with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on high-level interactions between the two countries.
During the talks, Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that China-U.S. relations have for some time generally moved forward along the track of constructive strategic stability charted by the two heads of state, which helps meet the expectations of the international community.
Noting that head-of-state diplomacy is the anchor of China-U.S. relations, Wang said the two sides should prepare for the next stage of high-level exchanges in a spirit of equality, respect and mutual benefit, strengthen communication, advance cooperation, manage differences, respect each other's core interests, and send a positive message that the two countries are committed to advancing a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability and jointly promoting world peace and development.
Wang also exchanged views with Rubio on the Middle East situation and other issues.

item.title: Trump says he is approaching major crossroads in Iran war: report
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
Demonstrators holding placards take part in a May Day rally in Los Angeles, California, the United States, on May 1, 2026. (Photo by Qiu Chen/Xinhua)
WASHINGTON, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is approaching a critical juncture in the Iran war over whether to resume massive attacks to bring the conflict to a close, U.S. online news outlet Axios reported.
"I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me," Trump told Axios.
Though Trump has made similar threats before, his comments came ahead of a planned meeting next Tuesday with leaders from six Gulf countries on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, said the report, adding that the meeting could shape the next phase of the war, including whether to make another push for diplomacy or intensify military action.
The six Gulf countries are Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman.
If Trump wants to resume major combat operations, he would need the support of his regional allies, the report said. Trump has said several times in recent days that the war will end soon.
The report also quoted some U.S. officials who warned that the conflict has settled into an unsustainable, neither-war-nor-peace stalemate, and that they believe Trump could return to major combat operations after the midterms if a deal is not reached by then.

item.title: Japanese PM Takaichi reshuffles cabinet, retains key ministers, taps first JIP member
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and members of her reshuffled Cabinet arrive at the prime minister’s office in Tokyo on September 17, 2026. /VCG
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi reshuffled her cabinet on Thursday, retaining most key ministers while bringing in a newcomer from the Japan Innovation Party (JIP), the junior coalition partner of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP).
It is Takaichi's first cabinet reshuffle since she took office last October.
According to the new lineup, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi, Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama all remained in their respective posts.
Among those entering the cabinet for the first time, House of Representatives members Kazuo Yana and Yoshihiro Seki had previously been disciplined by the LDP over a high-profile political slush fund scandal. They were named agriculture minister and education minister, respectively. This marked the first time since the scandal came to light that lawmakers disciplined by the party over the affair had received cabinet positions.
Hiroshi Nakatsuka, formerly secretary general of the JIP, was appointed minister in charge of regulatory reform, making him the first JIP member to serve as a cabinet minister. The move marked a shift from the LDP and JIP cooperating outside the cabinet to cooperation within the cabinet.
Shigeaki Koga, a former official at Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, said that on foreign and security policies, the JIP is even more hawkish than Takaichi and could potentially encourage the prime minister to pursue more hawkish policies.
Another focus of the reshuffle is the absence of former Internal Affairs and Communications Minister Yoshimasa Hayashi from the new cabinet. Hayashi was Takaichi's rival in last year's LDP presidential election.
Analysts said the personnel changes indicate, on the one hand, that the Takaichi administration will press ahead with its established military buildup, proactive fiscal policy, and diplomatic agenda.
The Takaichi government is set to revise Japan's three key security documents by the end of this year, potentially including plans to acquire large numbers of unmanned systems and move toward mass production of hypersonic missiles.
On the other hand, Takaichi's latest cabinet reshuffle is also aimed at consolidating her administration's power base and paving the way for her to secure another term as LDP president in next autumn's party leadership race.

item.title: China aims to cement its place at forefront of biomedical innovation with new 5-year plan
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
BEIJING, Sept. 18 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday released a five-year plan for its pharmaceutical industry, outlining targets such as keeping biomedical research, development, and application at the global forefront by 2030. This move signals the country's resolve to turn drug innovation into a strategic strength.
The plan, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and nine other authorities, calls for a major leap in the core competitiveness and international influence of China's pharmaceutical industry from 2026 to 2030. It is hoped that core technologies in key fields will see systematic breakthroughs during this period.
Specifically, first-in-class drugs developed in China should account for no less than 25 percent of the global total, with the number of innovative drugs approved for market ranking among the world leaders. The innovative drug sector is expected to grow at an average annual rate of at least 20 percent, according to the plan.
China also expects the biomedical sector to take shape as a national pillar industry at an accelerated pace.
The combined revenue of pharmaceutical enterprises above a designated scale threshold -- an annual main business revenue of 20 million yuan (about 2.96 million U.S. dollars) -- should reach at least 3.5 trillion yuan by 2030, the plan says.
The number of companies with an annual revenue exceeding 10 billion yuan should grow to 50. At least five Chinese drugs should achieve global annual sales exceeding 1 billion U.S. dollars, according to the plan.
The plan arrives at a pivotal moment as China's pharmaceutical industry is shifting rapidly from its traditional identity as a supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients and a large consumption market, toward a new phase defined by the export of innovative drugs.
In the first half of this year, 38 innovative drugs were approved in China, of which 31, or more than 80 percent, were domestically developed. As of the end of 2025, China had 4,751 innovative drugs in the pipeline, accounting for one third of the global total and placing it first in the world for drugs under development.
The broader industry also showed great vitality. Value-added output of China's pharmaceutical enterprises above the 20-million-yuan revenue threshold grew 6.4 percent year on year in the first half of this year.
Moreover, China's innovative drugs have gained wider global reach. The total value of overseas licensing deals for innovative Chinese drugs has surpassed 120 billion U.S. dollars this year, up 36 percent year on year.

item.title: Beyond expo floor, AI opens new frontiers in China-ASEAN cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
*China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) both aim to expand AI's role in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars last year.
*In the first seven months of 2026, China-ASEAN trade rose 24.7 percent year on year to 744.41 billion dollars, Chinese customs data show, as AI use expands in marketing, agriculture, logistics and finance.
*The distinction between technology that draws a crowd and technology that delivers real value is central to the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and the China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit, slated from Sept. 17 to 21 in Nanning, Guangxi's capital.
NANNING, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- Wei Qiaomei, a Chinese livestreamer, once struggled to grasp what her Thai customers wanted, though she speaks fluent Thai.
Once, ahead of her pitch for a portable fan, AI analyzed Thai e-commerce data and popped up two selling points for her: quiet motors and long battery life.
The trial has proven rewarding. Her employer, based in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, reported a 300 percent sales jump.
"Speaking the language isn't the same as understanding the market," said the 23-year-old, noting that AI had transformed her from a mere translator into a market-savvy presenter.
Her story reflects a broader shift in relations between China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), as both sides aim to expand AI's role in bilateral trade, which exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars last year.
This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a view of the Nanning International Convention and Exhibition Center, the venue for the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo, in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.(Xinhua/Zhou Hua)
FROM SHOWCASE TO APPLICATION
The event brings together more than 3,400 companies, with Timor-Leste attending for the first time as ASEAN's 11th member and an official co-host.
The expo's inaugural "AI marketplace" features about 500 products from more than 70 companies across eight categories, such as wearables, health management, and consumer technology, allowing visitors to test and buy items on-site.
"Last year, AI was mostly for show. This year, it is driving sales," said Wang Jicai, secretary-general of the China-ASEAN Expo Secretariat.
For Wei, the results are clear. Her company trained its model on ASEAN languages, local preferences, and cultural nuances, enabling it to analyze products, process reviews, and draft localized scripts. Livestream hosts then decide when to pivot, how to handle tough questions, and what to emphasize.
"AI didn't replace me. It amplified what I could do," Wei said.
Beyond the livestream studio, AI applications are being deployed in several ASEAN markets.
In Laos and Cambodia, a platform developed by a Guangxi enterprise and local partners uses satellite imagery, drones, and ground sensors to track pests and guide tropical crop cultivation.
The system, built with Chinese technology, local field data and training support, has been tested on more than 20,000 mu (about 1,333 hectares) of crops, said project head Wen Biaotang.
Visitors take photos of a humanoid robot performing tea ceremony during the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, Sept. 17, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhou Hua)
CROSS-BORDER DEPLOYMENT NARROWS AI DIVIDE
In Guangxi's border city Chongzuo, the center for disease control and prevention has partnered with neighboring Vietnamese provinces to deploy a bilingual AI platform for early disease detection.
It can slash epidemiological reporting time from four hours to 30 minutes, the project manager said.
In Nanning, RunDo, a platform operated by Runjian Co. Ltd., monitors almost 300 megawatts of solar capacity across nearly 3,000 sites in Malaysia remotely, with drones and AI replacing manual inspections.
"The platform has boosted maintenance efficiency by over 30 percent, raised power output by up to 5 percent, and cut labor costs by more than 20 percent," said Yang Yexi, marketing manager of the operator's Guangxi branch.
Leveraging Nanning's computing infrastructure, ASEAN companies can avoid building large intelligent computing centers and remotely access models and computing power for their business needs, Yang said, whose company has launched more than 80 computing projects across ASEAN.
These cases highlight the prerequisites for cross-border AI deployment: computing power, local data, skilled workers, and capable local partners.
Guangxi's China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, opened 279 to developers, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos, and Malaysia, backed more than 30 cross-border projects, and assembled an alliance of 55 companies.
To address the low-resource challenge faced by some Southeast Asian languages, a training base in Malaysia has logged more than 1,900 hours of multilingual data annotation, while a six-month regional competition attracted more than 200 teams.
Liu Jianmin, a professor at the School of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence of Guangxi University of Finance and Economics, said ASEAN universities, companies, and professionals could contribute to collecting, labeling and updating data if AI models are to work locally.
"No matter how accurate a system is, if no one uses it, can afford it, or can keep it running, it remains just an exhibit," Liu said.
The challenge is acute for ASEAN's smaller economies.
Without collective action, the cost of cybersecurity, data governance, and reliable AI frameworks could deepen an "intelligence divide," said Miguel Marques Goncalves Manetelu, Timor-Leste's minister of transport and communications.
This photo taken on Sept. 17, 2026 shows a scene of the opening ceremony of the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo and China-ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in Nanning, south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Cao Yiming)
FROM MATCHMAKING TO RULE-MAKING
Before the expo opened, an AI system had generated more than 8,000 buyer-seller matches and arranged nearly 2,000 face-to-face meetings.
According to the summit's organizers, the system provides real-time tariff and compliance guidance during negotiations, and tracks leads after the exhibition.
But, it still can not establish cross-border data protocols, guarantee electronic signatures, or assign liability when an algorithm fails.
AI can turn industrial expertise into a service that can be sold and delivered over time, said Meng Shuang, an associate professor of international economics at the Central University of Finance and Economics in Beijing.
Companies, she said, will increasingly package hardware, software, models, and long-term maintenance, with competitive advantage extending to algorithms, sector expertise, and local operating ability.
This evolution has pushed regional trade into more complex territory: data governance, AI service pricing and billing rules, electronic authentication, and intellectual property.
"Cross-border data flows are the lifeblood of AI," said ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn, who called for a trusted, secure, and seamless framework for data exchange.
The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, signed in October 2025, sets out a regional framework covering the digital and green economies, cross-border data flows, personal privacy, digital payments, and AI standards.
Standardized electronic authentication, interoperable payments, and joint data frameworks would first benefit sectors such as cross-border e-commerce, smart logistics, and industrial inspection, Meng added.
Ge Hongliang, a researcher at the School of Southeast Asian Studies at Guangxi Minzu University, said that cooperation among free-trade zones and ports under the upgraded protocol could support investment, data sharing, and intellectual-property protection.
To that end, this year's expo is hosting its first high-level dialogue on aligning Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) and China-ASEAN FTA rules.
For livestreamers like Wei, it comes down to knowing which fan feature matters most to a customer hundreds of miles away.

item.title: U.S. returns 64 cultural relics, fossils to China
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
NEW YORK, Sept. 17 (Xinhua) -- The United States has returned 64 Chinese cultural relics and paleontological fossils to China, China's National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) said Thursday.
The items were handed over in two batches in Washington and New York on Wednesday and Thursday by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and the Manhattan District Attorney's Office, respectively.
At the return ceremonies, Rao Quan, vice minister of Culture and Tourism and administrator of the NCHA, signed the confirmation of the return and receipt on behalf of the Chinese side.
The returned items, seized by U.S. law enforcement agencies, include the torso of a bodhisattva statue from the Tianlongshan Grottoes, as well as statues, terracotta figures, dinosaur skeleton fossils, fish fossils and dinosaur egg fossils.
The NCHA said that it worked with Chinese diplomatic and consular missions in the United States and relevant U.S. authorities to facilitate the return of the artifacts and that this week's return marked the fifth time the Manhattan District Attorney's Office had returned cultural relics to China.
The latest repatriations are part of China-U.S. cooperation to combat illicit trafficking of Chinese cultural property under a memorandum of understanding signed in 2009 and renewed three times since.
Present at the ceremonies were Chinese Ambassador to the United States Xie Feng and Consul General in New York Chen Li, along with representatives from the U.S. State Department, the HSI and the Manhattan District Attorney's Office.

item.title: 95 years on: Remembering September 18 Incident and lessons for peace
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-18
A ceremony is held to mark the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident in front of a monument at the September 18 Incident History Museum in Shenyang City, northeast China's Liaoning Province, September 18, 2026. /VCG
Sirens wailed and a bell tolled in northeast China on Friday to commemorate the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident, which marked the start of China's war of resistance against Japanese aggression.
Hundreds of people, including veterans and their relatives, gathered at the square of the 9.18 Historical Museum in Shenyang, capital of Liaoning Province, to honor those who fought in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression.
At exactly 9:18 a.m., 14 representatives from various sectors struck a huge bell 14 times, symbolizing the 14 years of bitter struggle against Japanese invaders.
Across the province, three minutes of air-raid sirens echoed, as pedestrians stood still in silent tribute.
Since 1995, Shenyang has sounded the air-raid alarm every year to commemorate the September 18 Incident.
On September 18, 1931, Japanese troops blew up a section of railway under their control near Shenyang and accused Chinese troops of sabotage as a pretext for their attack later that night against barracks near Shenyang, launching their premeditated invasion of China.
Veterans attend the ceremony for the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident at the September 18 Incident History Museum in Shenyang City, northeast China's Liaoning Province, September 18, 2026. /VCG
Preserving wartime memories through historical records
The 9.18 Historical Museum recently received a collection of precious historical relics donated by Zhan Hongge, a local collector.
The historical materials he donated include newspapers and periodicals published in China and abroad between 1931 and 1945, covering events such as the Japanese militarists' launch of the September 18 Incident, their occupation of northeast China, the resistance efforts of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army, and Japan’s announcement of its unconditional surrender.
Tian Jing, a research librarian at the museum, told China Media Group (CMG) that those newspapers and periodicals will provide valuable supplementary materials for our future research and exhibitions on the historical facts of the Northeast Anti-Japanese United Army led by the Communist Party of China.
Calls for historical reflection in Japan
In Tokyo, a number of Japanese history scholars and peace activists held a symposium on Wednesday to commemorate the 95th anniversary of the September 18 Incident. They shared views on war memory, accountability for wartime aggression and the passing down of ideals of peace at the symposium.
Takakage Fujita, secretary-general of the Association for Inheriting and Propagating the Murayama Statement, said the September 18 Incident had been concealed by the Japanese government for a long period during the war and only gradually became known to Japanese society through the Tokyo Trials, which came as a shock to many Japanese people.
In an interview with CGTN, Atsushi Koketsu, emeritus professor at Yamaguchi University in Japan, said Japan must apologize sincerely where apology is due as it seeks better relations with other countries.
Koketsu said he believes the September 18 Incident marked the beginning of Japan's path toward defeat.
Noting Japan deliberately used the term "incident" rather than war, Koketsu said it was not an "incident," it was a war fought without a declaration of war.
Acknowledging many of the most shameful chapters of history have been buried in darkness, Koketsu said scholars like him have a duty to pass on the truth of that war accurately to future generations.
"If we neglect that responsibility of preserving and transmitting its history, and if we deny, revise, fabricate,or distort the history of that war, that is the true guilt," he said.

item.title: Pinglu Canal's Madao Hub Showcases Smart, Green Ship Locks
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-16
A new gateway from China's inland waterways to the sea!
The Madao hub on the Pinglu Canal in Guangxi features giant water-saving locks and smart monitoring systems.
The 134.2-km canal will connect China's inland waterways with the Beibu Gulf, creating a shorter, more efficient route to the sea.
